analysis.one_liner: Lets workers form a union by majority sign-up, requires binding arbitration for a first contract, and increases penalties on employers who violate labor law.
analysis.headline: The Senate bill was introduced with 44 cosponsors (43 Democrats, 1 Republican) but never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current labor law, an employer can demand a private ballot election and can face only weak penalties for firing or threatening workers who try to unionize, and even after workers vote for a union, companies can stall a first contract indefinitely. This bill would have required the National Labor Relations Board to certify a union once a majority of workers sign authorization cards, without a second election; set timelines for negotiating a first contract that end in binding arbitration; and added real financial penalties (up to $20,000 per violation) plus back pay with doubled liquidated damages for employers who illegally fire or coerce workers during organizing drives [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Workers trying to organize unions and their families. Millions of employees lose their jobs or face retaliation each year for union activity; this bill makes union formation faster, first contracts easier to reach, and employer retaliation financially risky [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Would let the NLRB certify a union immediately once a majority of employees in a unit sign authorization cards, without directing an election [S2] [S3].
Would set a timeline for first contracts: 90 days of bargaining, then mediation, then binding arbitration for a two-year contract if no agreement is reached [S2] [S3].
Would give priority investigation to employer unfair labor practice charges during organizing drives and the first-contract period [S2] [S3].
Would add liquidated damages equal to twice back pay for workers discriminated against during organizing, plus civil penalties up to $20,000 per willful or repeated violation [S2] [S3].

Would shift the union-formation decision from a managed employer election campaign to a signature-collection process, reducing the employer's ability to use delay and captive-audience meetings to outlast organizing drives [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers who would face unionization or higher first-contract costs, particularly nonunion companies in low-wage, high-turnover sectors; they would lose the ability to demand a full election campaign, stall a first contract indefinitely, or fire union supporters with little financial consequence [S3].

drawbacks.text: Replacing a private-ballot election with a card-signing process removes the confidential vote that unions' critics argue protects workers from one-sided peer and organizer pressure [S3].

Binding arbitration imposes a contract written by an arbitrator rather than one negotiated by the parties, which critics say replaces bargaining with a government-imposed settlement for two years [S3].
Penalties up to $20,000 per violation plus triple back pay raise the cost of employment disputes and would be passed on in prices or absorbed in smaller payrolls [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would materially strengthen workers' ability to form unions and reach first contracts, at a real cost to employers in union-formation disputes and to workers who prefer a secret ballot. The private-ballot objection is the most serious good-faith objection; the doubled/tripled back pay and $20,000 penalties are targeted only at organizing-period violations, which limits the cost to firms that violate the law.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in April 2005 and referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where it never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended in early January 2007 [S1] [S5].

narrative.text: Sen. Edward Kennedy introduced S. 842 on April 19, 2005, with 35 original cosponsors listed on introduction [S3].
The Senate referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S5].
The committee took no recorded action; the bill never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote and died at the end of the 109th Congress on January 3, 2007 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have faced faster union formation, binding first-contract arbitration, and real penalties for illegal retaliation. They kept the status quo: elections they can manage, delays they can use, and penalties too small to change behavior. Working people who wanted to unionize got nothing from the 109th Congress. Burden falls on workers who want to unionize and on union supporters; benefit goes to employers who would have faced unionization, binding arbitration, and penalties. Employers won by default when the committee never acted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who would have faced unionization

for.name: Sen. Edward M. Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Introduced S. 842 on April 19, 2005, with 35 original cosponsors, and gave introductory remarks [S3] [S5].

for.name: 44 Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, including Sen. Arlen Specter (R-PA) as the sole Republican [S4] [S3].

for.name: American labor unions
for.what_they_did: Backed and campaigned for the Employee Free Choice Act, their top legislative priority of the period (widely reported; not documented in the provided record).

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.role: Senate majority party leadership of the 109th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor; with committee inaction, no floor consideration ever occurred (widely reported; the bill's failure to advance is documented in the record [S1] [S5]).

against.name: HELP Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Sen. Michael Enzi (R-WY)
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill — no hearing, no markup — after its April 2005 referral [S5].

against.name: Business and employer associations
against.what_they_did: Opposed the Employee Free Choice Act, arguing it would end the private ballot and impose binding arbitration (widely reported; not documented in the provided record).

sides.party_line_note: All 43 Democratic senators (at time of introduction) cosponsored alongside one Republican, Arlen Specter; with no hearing or vote ever scheduled, the only Republican cosponsor was Specter, and no recorded floor division occurred.

industries.industry: Employers in nonunion, low-wage, high-turnover sectors (retail, food service, warehousing, call centers)
industries.note: These employers lose the ability to demand a drawn-out election campaign and stall a first contract; they would face binding arbitration and up to $20,000 per violation plus triple back pay for illegal retaliation during organizing. Their gain from the bill dying is the status quo's weak enforcement, which is a cost to workers trying to organize.

industries.industry: Union-avoidance consultants and management-side labor law firms
industries.note: Card-check certification and binding arbitration shrink the market for anti-union campaigns and election litigation; the bill's death preserves their business.
Card-check would make organizing far easier and arbitration would end the first-contract stall; the bill's failure leaves unions with the existing slow, election-based process and weak remedies.
